# A Brief History of Lighthouses

For as long as people have sailed, they have needed a way to find land safely in the dark. The earliest aids were simple bonfires lit on hilltops, later raised onto platforms to extend their reach. From these beginnings grew one of the most enduring structures in maritime history.

The most famous ancient lighthouse was the Pharos of Alexandria, completed around 280 BCE under the Ptolemies. Rising perhaps 100 metres or more, it guided ships into Egypt's busiest harbour with a fire at its summit, possibly reflected by polished metal. It stood for well over a thousand years before earthquakes brought it down, and its name survives in the word for lighthouse in several languages, such as the French *phare* and Spanish *faro*. The Romans built widely on this model, erecting towers at Ostia, Dover, and La Coruña, where the Tower of Hercules still operates today.

After Rome's decline, lighthouse construction lapsed in Europe. Medieval lights were often tended by monks or maintained by port towns, burning wood, coal, or candles. Revival came with the expansion of trade. France's Cordouan lighthouse, finished in 1611, combined a working beacon with palatial architecture.

The eighteenth century brought the challenge of building on wave-swept rocks. The Eddystone reef off Plymouth saw a succession of towers: Henry Winstanley's wooden structure was destroyed in the Great Storm of 1703, taking its designer with it, and its successor burned. John Smeaton's 1759 tower solved the problem with interlocking granite blocks, hydraulic lime, and a curved profile modelled on an oak trunk. His design became the template for rock lighthouses worldwide, later refined by the Stevenson family in Scotland at sites such as Bell Rock and Skerryvore.

Illumination improved in parallel. Aimé Argand's hollow-wick oil lamp of the 1780s gave a steady, bright flame, and parabolic reflectors concentrated it. The decisive advance came in 1822, when Augustin-Jean Fresnel developed a lens of concentric prisms that gathered light into a powerful beam visible for many miles. Rotating lenses gave each station a distinctive flash pattern, allowing mariners to identify their position.

The nineteenth and twentieth centuries added kerosene, gas, and finally electricity, along with fog signals and radio beacons. Automation then gradually ended the lonely profession of the keeper; most lights were unmanned by the close of the twentieth century.

Today satellite navigation has reduced the lighthouse's practical importance, yet many remain in service as dependable backups. Others are preserved as museums and monuments, lasting symbols of vigilance and safe passage.
